quote: 8.1 By Commerce One. Commerce One shall indemnify, defend and hold harmless Corio and its Customers from any and all damages, liabilities, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) incurred by Corio or its Customers arising out of any claim that the Software infringes any patent, copyright, trademark or trade right secret of a third party
rationale: Section 8.1 gives us (Corio, as licensee/customer) a full defend-and-indemnify from Commerce One (the vendor/licensor) covering third-party claims that the Software infringes patent, copyright, trademark or trade secret rights, and extends to our Customers. It carries the standard procedure (prompt notice, tender of control/defence and settlement to Commerce One at its expense, our cooperation at its expense, with a right to join with our own counsel) and the usual remedy ladder in Section 8.1/p0087 (procure the right, replace or modify, or terminate and refund a pro-rated portion of fees paid). The Section 8.2 exclusions (use other than as documented; third-party modification where the infringement would not have occurred but for the modification) are the usual customer-modification/specification carve-outs. There is no reciprocal Corio indemnity anywhere in the agreement, so the one-way structure runs in our favour, and Section 9 expressly carves "LIABILITY ARISING UNDER SECTION 8" out of both the 12-month fee cap and the consequential-damages exclusion, leaving the vendor indemnity uncapped — better than the fallback's 3x annual fees super-cap. The clause therefore meets the fallback (and on the cap point exceeds it). Noted but not flagged as deviations: the indemnity is limited to IP infringement and does not extend to Commerce One's breach of applicable law, unauthorised access to or disclosure of our data, or its gross negligence/wilful misconduct as the preferred position would provide; the refund remedy is limited to a pro-rated portion of fees paid. These are sub-elements short of preferred wording, not material failures of the fallback, so no redline is proposed.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have deleted the carve-out that transfers ownership of Developments created solely by Corio to Commerce One where Commerce One supports them on an ongoing basis, since our playbook does not permit any assignment of our IP or work product to a vendor, and the carve-out gave us no licence back. If Commerce One needs rights in Developments it maintains, we can instead grant it a licence to those Developments while ownership stays with Corio.

ops.newText: shall be owned by Corio, including all
ops.oldText: shall be owned by Corio, unless such Developments are supported on an ongoing basis by Commerce One in which case Commerce One will retain all ownership rights, including

ops.newText: intellectual property rights therein. To the extent
ops.oldText: intellectual property rights in the Developments. To the extent

proposal.summary: Remove vendor ownership carve-out so Corio owns all Developments it creates.

quote: shall be owned by Corio, unless such Developments are supported on an ongoing basis by Commerce One in which case Commerce One will retain all ownership rights, including
rationale: Section 13.5 starts from the preferred position (Developments created solely by Corio are owned by Corio, with Commerce One assigning any claim it may have, and Commerce One retaining its pre-existing technology under 2.8 — vendor platform ownership is acceptable). However, the "unless" carve-out flips ownership of our own work product to Commerce One whenever Commerce One supports it on an ongoing basis, with no licence back to Corio. That is an assignment of Customer IP to the Vendor and fails even the fallback (which requires at minimum a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to use the deliverables), so it is walk-away territory on a critical term. The smallest edit to reach the preferred position is deletion of the carve-out; if Commerce One needs rights in Developments it maintains, a licence from Corio rather than ownership is the sensible fallback. Noted but not separately flagged: the final sentence of 13.5 leaves ownership of enhancements to the Software itself to future negotiation (no joint ownership is created), and the agreement has no Customer Data ownership sentence, a minor sub-element in this hosting/reseller structure.
ruleTitle: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have changed the cap from amounts paid for the single related transaction to the greater of the fees paid or payable in the preceding twelve months and US$1,000,000, since a per-transaction cap is not a meaningful remedy for us. We have also added the standard carve-outs so that confidentiality, indemnification, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement sit outside the cap; we can drop the US$1,000,000 floor if the carve-outs are agreed.

ops.newText: EXCEED THE GREATER OF (A) THE TOTAL AMOUNT PAID OR PAYABLE BY CORIO HEREUNDER DURING THE TWELVE (12) MONTHS IMMEDIATELY PRIOR TO THE EVENT GIVING RISE TO THE LIABILITY AND (B) ONE MILLION U.S. DOLLARS (US$1,000,000). THE FOREGOING LIMITATION SHALL NOT APPLY TO A PARTY'S BREACH OF ITS CONFIDENTIALITY OBLIGATIONS, ITS INDEMNIFICATION OBLIGATIONS, ITS GROSS NEGLIGENCE, WILLFUL MISCONDUCT OR FRAUD, OR ITS INFRINGEMENT OF THE OTHER PARTY'S INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS, OR TO CORIO'S OBLIGATION TO PAY FEES DUE HEREUNDER.
ops.oldText: EXCEED THE TOTAL AMOUNT ACTUALLY PAID BY CORIO HEREUNDER FOR THE TRANSACTION WHICH THE LIABILITY RELATES TO DURING THE TWELVE (12) MONTHS IMMEDIATELY PRIOR TO THE FILING OF THE CAUSE OF ACTION TO WHICH THE LIABILITY RELATES.

proposal.summary: Make the cap an aggregate 12-month fees / US$1,000,000 floor and add carve-outs for confidentiality, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement

quote: IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY'S LIABILITY ARISING OUT OF THIS AGREEMENT OR THE USE OR PERFORMANCE OF THE SOFTWARE EXCEED THE TOTAL AMOUNT ACTUALLY PAID BY CORIO HEREUNDER FOR THE TRANSACTION WHICH THE LIABILITY RELATES TO DURING THE TWELVE (12) MONTHS IMMEDIATELY PRIOR TO THE FILING OF THE CAUSE OF ACTION TO WHICH THE LIABILITY RELATES.
rationale: The cap is mutual and the consequential-damages exclusion is mutual, but the cap fails the fallback on two material terms. First, the basis is not 12 months' fees: it is limited to amounts "actually paid by Corio ... for the transaction which the liability relates to", which slices the cap down to a single transaction's fees and can fall well below six months' fees for Commerce One — walk-away territory. Second, the only carve-out is Section 8 (Commerce One's IP indemnity); there is no carve-out for breach of confidentiality (Section 10 / the concurrent NDA), gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud, all of which the fallback requires. We therefore moved the cap to the greater of 12 months' fees paid or payable and US$1,000,000, added the standard carve-out sentence, and confirmed Corio's payment obligations are not subject to the cap. The US$1,000,000 floor is the preferred position and can be dropped as a fallback if the carve-outs are accepted.
ruleTitle: Limitation of liability — cap, mutuality and carve-outs

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have added an intra-group (affiliate) carve-out and a "not unreasonably withheld" standard to the consent requirement, so neither party can block a routine internal reorganisation on an arbitrary basis. The existing merger/asset-sale carve-out and the direct-competitor exception are unchanged.

ops.newText: Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement, without such consent, to any entity controlling, controlled by or under common control with such party, or in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement,
ops.oldText: Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement without such consent,

proposal.summary: Add affiliate carve-out and a reasonableness standard to the mutual assignment consent right in Section 14.1.

quote: Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement without such consent, except in the case where such transaction involves a direct competitor of the other party where consent of the other party will be required.
rationale: Section 14.1 is mutual and does contain an M&A/asset-sale carve-out, so it is not in walk-away territory, and there is no change-of-control termination or re-pricing right anywhere in the agreement (Section 11 termination triggers are limited to uncured material breach and insolvency). However, the fallback position requires that consent for assignments outside the successor carve-out be subject to a "not unreasonably withheld" standard, and this clause gives each party an unfettered discretion to refuse; there is also no carve-out for intra-group (affiliate) transfers, which the preferred position requires for us. We therefore made the minimal edit to add an affiliate carve-out and a reasonableness standard, leaving the mutual competitor exception intact. Minor point noted only: the successor carve-out is limited to assets "related to this Agreement", which we accept.

quote: 2.1 Hosting Software License. Subject to the terms and conditions of this Agreement, Commerce One hereby grants to Corio a fee-bearing, perpetual and irrevocable, nonexclusive, nontransferable (except in accordance with Section 14.1 of this Agreement), right and license in the Territory to (i) reproduce the Software in machine executable object code format only for installation on the Corio Servers;
rationale: The agreement imposes no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation on Corio (our party). All licences in Section 2 are expressly "nonexclusive" and run in our favour; Section 2.7 restricts only copying/reverse engineering of the Software, not our freedom to source competing procurement or hosting software from third parties. Section 2.4 in fact operates in our favour by barring Commerce One from contacting Corio Customers for non-ASP licence sales and requiring referrals to us. Section 13 (Shared Resources) and the CORIO MARKET SEGMENT definition (Section 1.3) limit customer segment and territory scope but contain no requirements/exclusive-dealing covenant, and Exhibit D sales and marketing cooperation is expressly stated to be "non-binding" (p0198), so the cross-selling and joint marketing commitments create no enforceable soft exclusivity. This meets the preferred position (no exclusivity obligation on the customer); no redline needed.

quote: the nonbreaching party may terminate this Agreement on written notice at any time following the end of such-thirty (30) day period.
rationale: The Agreement contains no liquidated damages, penalty, late-payment interest, minimum-shortfall or early-termination fee payable by Corio. Fees (Sections 4.1–4.4, Exhibit B pricing and Exhibit B payment terms) are limited to license, maintenance/support, MarketSite.net access, implementation and revenue-share amounts actually earned, and termination under Section 11.2 triggers no exit or minimum payment — only survival of ongoing payment obligations for continued use and support, which is consideration rather than a penalty. This meets the preferred position (no liquidated damages or penalties payable by the customer), so no redline is warranted. Amounts running the other way (Commerce One's MarketSite transaction revenue share to Corio in Exhibit B and its support obligations in Exhibit C) benefit us and are not flagged.
ruleTitle: Liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have added a short subsection confirming that the Section 2 licences extend to our affiliates and to contractors acting on our behalf, with Corio remaining responsible for their compliance, since the grant as drafted is limited to Corio alone and Section 2.7 bars any other access. If preferred, we can instead cover affiliates on written notice to Commerce One.

ops.text: 2.11 Affiliates and Contractors. The licenses granted to Corio under this Section 2 extend to Corio's affiliates (meaning any entity that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with Corio) and to contractors acting on Corio's behalf, in each case subject to the terms and conditions of this Agreement. Corio shall remain responsible for such affiliates' and contractors' compliance with this Agreement.

proposal.summary: Extend the Section 2 licences to Corio's affiliates and to contractors acting on Corio's behalf

quote: 2.1 Hosting Software License. Subject to the terms and conditions of this Agreement, Commerce One hereby grants to Corio a fee-bearing, perpetual and irrevocable, nonexclusive, nontransferable (except in accordance with Section 14.1 of this Agreement), right and license in the Territory to (i) reproduce the Software in machine executable object code format only for installation on the Corio Servers;
rationale: The grant is perpetual and irrevocable (2.1) and the paid-up internal-use licence is perpetual (2.3/2.2), and Section 14.1 permits assignment to a successor in a merger, acquisition or asset sale, so the irrevocability and successor-transfer elements meet the playbook. However, every licence in Section 2 runs to "Corio" only: affiliates are never mentioned anywhere in the Agreement, contractors are not covered (only "Corio Servers" contemplates operation "by or for Corio"), and Section 2.7 expressly bars allowing access except as explicitly permitted, so there is no path to add affiliates or contractors. That fails the fallback (affiliates covered on written notice) on a material term, so we add a short subsection extending the Section 2 licences to affiliates and to contractors acting on our behalf, with Corio remaining responsible for their compliance. Minor point noted only: the 14.1 assignment right carries a direct-competitor consent carve-out, which we accept.

quote: 13.6 Independent Development: Covenant not to Sue. Nothing in this Agreement will be construed to prohibit either parties' right to independently develop the Developments contemplated above.
rationale: The agreement contains no non-compete, exclusivity or field-of-use covenant binding Corio (our party). Section 2.7 (p0042) is a conventional license-scope/IP-use restriction on copying, reverse engineering and use of Commerce One's Software, not a restraint on the businesses Corio may operate or the products it may buy or build; Section 13.6 (p0117) expressly preserves each party's right to develop independently. The "Territory" and "Corio Market Segment" definitions (p0024, p0013) limit the scope of the licenses Commerce One grants (and p0013 even confirms Corio's right to keep serving customers that grow past the revenue threshold, with above-threshold opportunities to be discussed) rather than restricting Corio's own business or its freedom to use competing products; Exhibit D marketing cooperation is expressly non-binding. This meets the preferred position (no non-compete or field-of-use restriction on Customer), so no redline is proposed.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement runs an initial five (5) year term but gives us no exit other than for breach or insolvency, so we have added a convenience termination right on thirty (30) days' notice with a refund of prepaid fees, consistent with our playbook position. If a longer runway is needed we can move to 60-90 days' notice.

ops.text: 11.3 Termination for Convenience. Corio may terminate this Agreement for convenience, in whole or in part, upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One, without penalty or early termination charge, in which case Commerce One shall refund to Corio any prepaid fees allocable to the period after the effective date of such termination. Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term.

proposal.summary: Add Corio right to terminate for convenience on 30 days' notice with pro-rata refund of prepaid fees; no Commerce One convenience right mid-term.

quote: 11.1 Term. The term of this Agreement shall commence on the Effective Date and shall continue in full force and effect for an initial period of five (5) years. Thereafter, this Agreement shall automatically renew for subsequent one (1) year periods unless either party provides the other party with written notification at least thirty (30) days prior to the expiration of the initial five (5) year term or any one (1) year renewal thereof of its intention to terminate this Agreement.
rationale: Section 11 creates a five-year committed term with automatic one-year renewals, and the only termination triggers in Section 11.2 are uncured material breach and insolvency. The 30-day notice in Section 11.1 is a non-renewal mechanic exercisable only at the end of a term, not a convenience exit. Corio therefore has no right to terminate for convenience at any point during a multi-year term, which the playbook treats as walk-away territory and a material failure of the fallback (which requires at least a 60-90 day customer convenience right). Commerce One likewise holds no convenience right, so no vendor-side exit needs deleting, and Sections 4 and 17 contain no early-termination fee or fee-acceleration mechanic. Redline inserts a new Section 11.3 giving Corio a 30-day convenience right with refund of prepaid fees and confirms Commerce One has no mid-term convenience exit; the 60-90 day fallback is offered in the comment.

quote: Such books and records shall be kept for at least three (3) years following the end of the calendar month to which they pertain, and shall be open for inspection by an independent certified public accountant reasonably acceptable to Corio for the purpose of verifying the amounts payable to Commerce One under this Agreement. Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year, at reasonable times and upon reasonable notice. Commerce One shall bear all costs and expenses of such inspection.
rationale: Section 4.4 is the only audit/verification right binding Corio (our party), and it substantially meets the preferred position: audits are limited to once each calendar year, must be conducted at reasonable times and on reasonable notice, may be performed only by an independent CPA reasonably acceptable to Corio, and Commerce One bears all costs unless an underpayment exceeding 5% is found. There is no right of direct or remote access to Corio systems — only books and records relating to amounts payable — so no walk-away trigger. Minor points short of preferred wording, noted but not redlined: notice is "reasonable" rather than a fixed 30 (or fallback 15) days and in writing, and the auditor is not expressly stated to be bound by confidentiality obligations.

quote: This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of California, USA, excluding conflict of laws provisions and excluding the 1980 United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. Any disputes arising out of this Agreement shall be resolved by binding arbitration in accordance with the then-current commercial arbitration rules of the American Arbitration Association ("RULES"). The arbitration shall be conducted by one (1) arbitrator appointed in accordance with the Rules in San Francisco County, California.
rationale: Section 14.3 is the governing law, arbitration and venue clause. Governing law is California, which sits squarely within the playbook's fallback list (Delaware or California law and courts), and the dispute forum is domestic — AAA arbitration seated in San Francisco County, California, with judgment enforceable in the courts of San Francisco. There is no foreign seat and no exclusive foreign venue, so the walk-away trigger (vendor home jurisdiction outside the accepted list, or mandatory arbitration seated abroad) is not engaged. California is also the home jurisdiction of both parties here, so the forum is convenient for us rather than adverse. Noted but not flagged: the playbook prefers New York law with the state and federal courts of New York County, and prefers courts over arbitration; single-arbitrator AAA arbitration in an accepted US jurisdiction is a sub-preferred mechanic rather than a material failure of the fallback. The loser-pays allocation of AAA fees is symmetrical and not adverse to us. Accordingly the clause is compliant at the fallback and we do not redline it.

quote: 4.1 License Fees. In consideration for the licenses granted to Corio pursuant to Section 2 of this Agreement, Corio shall pay the license fees specified in EXHIBIT B hereto. Payment terms of such license fees shall be as set forth in EXHIBIT B hereto.
rationale: No most-favoured-nation or price/terms-matching obligation exists anywhere in the Agreement. Searches for "most favored/favourable", "no less favorable", "lowest", "best price", "discount", "similarly situated" and "other customers" returned nothing, and the only pricing, revenue-sharing and payment provisions (Section 4 Fees, Exhibit B Pricing/Revenue Sharing Fees, Exhibit B Payment Terms) set fixed fees, fixed revenue shares and fixed payment timing with no obligation on Corio to extend Commerce One terms given to third parties or to match third-party offers. Section 2 (Grant of Rights) and Exhibit D (Sales and Marketing Cooperation, expressly non-binding) likewise impose no MFN-type undertaking; Section 2.9/2.10 leave future products and geographic expansion to mutual agreement rather than benchmarked terms. This meets the preferred position (no MFN obligation on the customer), so there is nothing to redline.

quote: 4.1 License Fees. In consideration for the licenses granted to Corio pursuant to Section 2 of this Agreement, Corio shall pay the license fees specified in EXHIBIT B hereto.
rationale: No minimum purchase commitment, take-or-pay or shortfall penalty is imposed on Corio. Fees are limited to (i) the licence fees for the licences actually granted (§4.1, Exhibit B), (ii) annual maintenance and MarketSite.net access fees for services actually provided (§4.2, Exhibit B Payment Terms), (iii) implementation fees on a time-and-materials basis capped by the Statement of Work, and (iv) revenue-share on a percentage of Application Management Revenue actually invoiced to Corio Customers (p0157–p0159) — i.e. usage/ordered-services pricing, which meets the preferred position. Maintenance is expressly conditional ("provided that Corio continues to pay the annual Maintenance and Support fees"), so there is no committed multi-year spend. Two minor points noted but not flagged: the revenue-share carve-out for the initial 3000 user licences is "subject to a minimum limitation of 40 Authorized Software Users per Customer" (p0158), which is a counting convention for the free-of-revenue-share pool rather than a purchase commitment on us; and the five-year initial term in §11.1 has no convenience exit, which is a term-length point addressed under the term/termination rule rather than a take-or-pay commitment here. The "shortfall" reference in §4.4 is a mutual audit true-up, not a penalty.
ruleTitle: Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions on Customer

quote: 14.5 Independent Contractors. The parties are independent contractors with respect to each other. Each party is not and shall not be deemed to be an employee, agent, partner or legal representative of the other for any purpose and shall not have any right, power or authority to create any obligation or responsibility on behalf of the other.
rationale: Searches for "solicit", "hire", "employ" and "induce" return no restrictive covenant on personnel anywhere in the Agreement. The only personnel-related provisions are Section 13 (Shared Resources), which addresses access to Commerce One operations/consulting/engineering personnel, Employee NDA/Invention Agreements and ownership of Developments (p0116), Section 14.5 (independent contractors, p0126) and Exhibit D Section 5 (each party assigns a sales/marketing employee, p0203) — none of which restricts Corio from soliciting, hiring or engaging Commerce One personnel. This matches the preferred position of no non-solicit binding the Customer, so no redline is warranted.

quote: Thereafter, this Agreement shall automatically renew for subsequent one (1) year periods unless either party provides the other party with written notification at least thirty (30) days prior to the expiration of the initial five (5) year term or any one (1) year renewal thereof of its intention to terminate this Agreement.
rationale: Section 11.1 provides automatic renewals of one (1) year each — not multi-year — and either party (including us) may prevent renewal on just 30 days' written notice, which is within the preferred ≤30-day window and well inside the fallback (≤60 days) and walk-away (>90 days) thresholds. Renewal is symmetrical, so the exit right benefits us. Two preferred sub-elements are absent but are not material deviations: there is no Commerce One obligation to send a 60-day renewal reminder, and there is no express cap on renewal-period price increases (no uplift or escalation language appears anywhere, including the support and maintenance fee provisions, so no uncapped increase is granted either). We would note these in negotiation but they do not warrant a redline.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have added a transition and data-return provision: on expiry or termination Commerce One provides up to six months of transition assistance at its then-current rates, returns our and our Customers' data in a commonly used machine-readable format within thirty (30) days, and certifies deletion thereafter. Our playbook requires an orderly exit and return of our data; we can accept 90 days of assistance if six months is not workable.

ops.text: 11.4 Transition Assistance and Return of Data. Upon expiration or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Commerce One shall (a) at Corio's request, provide reasonable transition assistance to Corio and its Customers for a period of up to six (6) months at Commerce One's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days of Corio's request, return or make available to Corio all data of Corio, its Customers and Software Users then residing in the Software, the MarketSite.net Service or Commerce One's systems, in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete such data from its systems and certify such deletion to Corio in writing. This Section 11.4 shall survive any termination or expiration of this Agreement.

proposal.summary: Insert Section 11.4 requiring Commerce One to provide transition assistance and return Corio/Customer data on termination

quote: Upon termination or expiration of this Agreement, each party shall otherwise return or destroy any Confidential Information of the other party provided, however, Corio may retain any Confidential Information necessary for Corio to continue supporting it's then-existing Customers.
rationale: Section 11 contains term, termination and survival provisions but no post-termination transition assistance or data return/export obligation. Section 11.3 addresses only mutual return or destruction of Confidential Information (with a Corio carve-out) and continuity of Corio's sublicense rights and Commerce One's support obligations; Section 12's source code escrow provides some continuity of the Software but says nothing about returning Corio's or its Customers' data in a usable format, timing, or certified deletion. In a hosted arrangement where Commerce One operates the MarketSite.net Service, this falls short even of the fallback (90 days of assistance plus 30-day data export), so we insert a new Section 11.4 at the preferred position (up to six months of assistance at then-current rates, 30-day machine-readable return, certified deletion), with the 90-day fallback available in negotiation.
ruleTitle: Post-termination transition assistance and data return

proposal.comment: [Playbook] The 60-day warranty running from the Effective Date and expiring no later than December 31, 1999 would lapse at or before acceptance under Section 3.1, so we have extended it to twelve (12) months from acceptance and added a professional and workmanlike standard for Commerce One's services, consistent with our playbook position. We can accept ninety (90) days from acceptance as a fallback if the longer period is an issue.

ops.newText: for a period of twelve (12) months from Corio's acceptance of the Software pursuant to Section 3.1 (the "Warranty Period")
ops.oldText: for a period of sixty (60) days from the Effective Date, but in no event not later than December 31, 1999 (the "Warranty Period")

ops.text: Commerce One further warrants that all installation, implementation, training and other professional services provided under this Agreement will be performed in a professional and workmanlike manner consistent with industry standards, and that Corio's remedy for breach of this warranty shall be re-performance of the non-conforming services or, if Commerce One is unable to re-perform them within thirty (30) days, a refund of the fees paid for such services.

proposal.summary: Extend software/service warranty to 12 months from acceptance (removing the December 31, 1999 cut-off) and add a professional and workmanlike services warranty.

quote: Commerce One warrants that the Software and MarketSite.net Service will perform in substantial accordance with the Documentation, and the media on which the Software is distributed will be free from defects in materials and workmanship under normal use, for a period of sixty (60) days from the Effective Date, but in no event not later than December 31, 1999 (the "Warranty Period").
rationale: There is an express conformance-to-Documentation warranty with repair/replace and, failing that, termination plus refund of prepaid fees, and a no-malicious-code warranty, so the remedy structure meets the playbook. The duration fails the fallback: the warranty runs only sixty (60) days from the Effective Date and in no event past December 31, 1999, whereas Acceptance Testing under Section 3.1 itself runs to December 31, 1999 — so the warranty would expire at or before acceptance, well short of even the 90-day software fallback. The redline sets a twelve (12) month period measured from acceptance and removes the calendar cut-off, and adds a professional and workmanlike warranty for Commerce One's installation, implementation and other professional services (currently absent). We note separately that the disclaimer text (p0084) appears truncated in this copy; on its face it disclaims only implied warranties and does not swallow the express warranties.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement has no insurance covenant even though Commerce One places consultants on site and its MarketSite.net Service handles Corio and Customer data, so we have added our standard insurance provision (USD 1M/2M CGL, USD 2M E&O, USD 5M cyber, statutory workers' compensation, certificates on request) and the following subsection renumbers. If these limits are an issue, we can fall back to USD 1,000,000 errors and omissions and USD 2,000,000 cyber liability coverage.

ops.text: 14.10 Insurance. Commerce One shall maintain, at its own expense, throughout the term of this Agreement and for one (1) year thereafter: (a) commercial general liability insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000 per occurrence and USD 2,000,000 in the aggregate; (b) professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than USD 2,000,000; (c) where Commerce One processes Corio or Customer data, cyber liability insurance of not less than USD 5,000,000; and (d) workers' compensation insurance as required by applicable law. Commerce One shall provide Corio with certificates of insurance upon request.

proposal.summary: Insert vendor insurance covenant (CGL, E&O, cyber) as new Section 14.10

quote: 14.9 Bankruptcy. The parties hereto agree that Corio, as a licensee of Commerce One's intellectual property, shall be afforded all of the protections afforded to a licensee under Section 365(n) of the United States Bankruptcy Code
rationale: A full-text search for "insurance" returns only the Net Revenue definition (p0012); neither the Miscellaneous section (14.1-14.10) nor the Indemnification section contains any insurance covenant, so no clause meets even the fallback (E&O USD 1M / cyber USD 2M). Commerce One is a vendor that touches our data and premises: it supplies an on-site operations consultant and professional services (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 5.6) and operates the MarketSite.net Service used by Corio and its Customers, so the absence of insurance is walk-away territory under the rule. Proposed insertion of a new Section 14.10 in Miscellaneous at the preferred limits (USD 1M/2M CGL, USD 2M E&O, USD 5M cyber, statutory workers' compensation, certificates on request), with the fallback limits offered in the comment; the existing 14.10 renumbers.
